Even $100 Million Mansions Are Considered Teardowns These Days
 
Plus, California homeowners rethink their backyards amid wildfires and a divorced couple finishes building their home despite breaking up
 
By Kerry Barger
 
 
A circa-1980s home in Palm Beach is on the market for $185 million. Though the house is in good condition, local agents say it will likely be demolished to make way for something more modern. JONAH HEINL/NEXT LISTING STUDIOS
 

This is an edition of the WSJ Homes newsletter, a weekly guide to luxurious properties, celebrity homes, interior design and the housing market. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 

We have officially entered the era of the $100 million-plus teardown.

 

It isn’t uncommon for the superrich to purchase and demolish older homes or those in need of a major renovation. Lately, they are tearing down relatively new houses—often after paying nine-figure sums—to build custom homes more in line with today’s styles.

 

“It would seem that these homes are beautiful and livable, with higher-end appliances, cabinetry, countertops, those types of things,” said Robert Burrage, a South Florida-based contractor who has worked on several uber-luxury homes. “But not to the guy who has $100 million and wants what he wants the way he wants it.”

 

At the center of this trend is Palm Beach, which has a high concentration of ultra high net worth individuals and a low supply of oceanfront homes for sale. “It’s logical that this would be an increasing phenomenon,” said real-estate appraiser Jonathan Miller. “As the land gets more expensive, the cost to replace the house drops as a percentage.”

 
 
In March 2023, cosmetics billionaire William P. Lauder paid $155 million for the longtime oceanfront estate of the late radio host Rush Limbaugh. By July, Lauder had demolished it. EAGLEVIEW
 

As California deals with mounting wildfire threats and shrinking insurance options, homeowners are increasingly clearing the perimeter around their homes. Known as Zone 0, this 0-to-5-foot buffer is meant to keep the area free of flammable materials, from plants and bark mulch to wooden fences, patio furniture, and even jute doormats.

 

Finally, a pair of homeowners wanted to build a home base for their kids in California. A few years into the $10.7 million project, the couple decided to split up—but instead of abandoning or selling the property, they pressed on together, keeping ownership in both of their names. “Nobody had to make a choice. It’s been a big part of our healing.”

 
 
 

The Superrich Are Buying $100 Million Mansions Just to Tear Them Down

 
 
PELICAN PIX
 

In elite enclaves like Palm Beach, billionaire buyers are demolishing even relatively new houses to secure prime lots for their own custom builds.

Californians Ward Off Wildfires by Trading Lush Lawns for Stone and Steel

 
 
A home in Rancho Santa Fe, Calif., has metal plant sculptures in a rock bed closest to the house, and real plants outside a low wall. ALEX LAWN/GREENWAY LANDSCAPE DESIGN AND BUILD
 

A proposed state mandate and shrinking insurance options are pushing homeowners to turn a critical 5-foot zone around their homes into a fire buffer.

 
 
 

What’s the Deal?

 
 
JUST PENDED MEDIA
 

In Alaska, a 147-acre compound about 40 miles outside Anchorage is hitting the market for $12.5 million. The property has a ranch-style main house and two-bedroom apartment, plus its own helipad.

 

Slack co-founder Stewart Butterfield and Away co-founder Jen Rubio have sold their Aspen, Colo., home for $30 million, shortly after announcing their split on Instagram.

 

A newly built waterfront estate in Naples has sold for $69.36 million, the latest in a string of major deals for the affluent coastal city in southwest Florida.

 

Want to see more deals? Sign up for our Mansion Deals email alert to have the biggest and best luxury home sales and listings delivered to your inbox.

 
 
 

The Luxe Life

 
 
GELOY CONCEPCION FOR WSJ
 

A divorced couple finished building their Palo Alto home to give their family an anchor after their split. “This is his home too. I wanted it to be home for everyone.”

 

Malcolm Gladwell received 25 rejection letters from advertising agencies before applying for an assistant managing editor position. “I applied, knowing nothing about it. Miraculously, I got the job and moved to the U.S.”

 
 
 

House of the Week

 
 
MARK WILSON
 

WSJ’s House of the Week brings readers to a 1930s French Normandy-style compound on a private island on the Canadian side of Rainy Lake.

 

“This House of the Week began with a tip from an unlikely source: my dad, while on a recent Rainy Lake fishing trip,” says Mansion reporter Jessica Flint. “Word on the water was that French Island was being shopped off-market. Back at camp, he did some digging and managed to track down the estate’s caretaker, who passed along my contact information to the owner.”
